strengths: Addressing wide field-of-view (fisheye and 360° spherical) imagery in feed-forward multi-view 3D foundation models is an important, practical, and underexplored problem in current visual geometry research.

The adaptation of the ray-based representation with spherical harmonics into a multi-view permutation-equivariant framework (decoupling angular rays and radial distances) is sensible, technically sound, and well-executed.

The experimental evaluation is extensive, spanning multiple tasks including zero-shot relative camera pose estimation, dense point map estimation, large-scale visual localization, and monocular depth estimation across challenging real-world fisheye and panoramic datasets (e.g., ScanNet++, Matterport3D, Stanford2D3D, FIORD).

Wid3R demonstrates substantial quantitative and qualitative improvements over existing state-of-the-art feed-forward models (such as VGGT and $\pi^3$) that fail under severe lens distortions and non-perspective projections.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is somewhat incremental, as the architecture heavily combines existing paradigms: the permutation-equivariant multi-view backbone and pose regression from $\pi^3$, and the spherical harmonics ray representation and camera augmentation from UniK3D.

The camera model token conditioning appears to rely on knowing the discrete camera category (e.g., pinhole, fisheye, 360°) beforehand. The paper does not thoroughly analyze the model's sensitivity or failure modes when an incorrect token is provided or when cameras possess intermediate/unusual distortion profiles and FoVs.

The paper does not report benchmark results on standard perspective pinhole datasets (e.g., standard ScanNet or CO3D) to assess whether adopting this general wide-FoV representation incurs any performance trade-offs or regression on standard perspective reconstruction compared to baseline models like $\pi^3$ or VGGT.

strengths: Addresses an important and practical shortcoming of current feed-forward 3D reconstruction foundation models (e.g., DUSt3R, VGGT, $\pi^3$), which are fundamentally biased towards perspective/pinhole images and degrade severely on wide field-of-view (fisheye and 360°) inputs.

The formulation nicely integrates a spherical harmonics-based ray representation with a permutation-equivariant multi-view backbone and camera model conditioning tokens, allowing unified multi-view reconstruction without explicit rectification or calibration.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across multiple tasks and benchmarks, including zero-shot camera pose estimation (FIORD, Zip-NeRF, Stanford2D3D), dense point map estimation (ScanNet++, Matterport3D, Stanford2D3D), visual localization, and monocular depth estimation.

Achieves convincing quantitative and qualitative improvements over state-of-the-art multi-view methods on distorted and omnidirectional imagery, showing strong feed-forward speed advantages over classic SfM pipelines.
weaknesses: The technical novelty is somewhat incremental as it primarily combines concepts from existing works: the spherical harmonics ray formulation, radial decomposition, asymmetric loss, and camera augmentation follow UniK3D [54], while the multi-view permutation-equivariant architecture, loss formulation, and scale alignment follow $\pi^3$ [80].

The framework requires the camera model category (pinhole, fisheye, or 360°) to be known a priori at inference to select the appropriate camera token $C_i$. An analysis of model robustness against token misspecification or continuous variations in field-of-view within a camera class is missing.

Distinction between zero-shot and within-dataset test splits could be clearer: Matterport3D and ScanNet++ are included in the training mixture (evaluated on held-out test splits), whereas Stanford2D3D, Zip-NeRF, and FIORD are zero-shot unseen datasets. The text should consistently make this separation explicit across all benchmark tables.

strengths: Addresses an important and practical limitation of current 3D foundation models (e.g., DUSt3R, VGGT, $\pi^3$), which inherently assume pinhole/rectified perspective cameras and perform poorly on wide-FoV (fisheye, equirectangular/360°) images.

The technical design effectively decouples geometry prediction into ray directions via spherical harmonics basis expansion and radial distances, paired with discrete camera model tokens to handle varied projection geometries within a permutation-equivariant multi-view architecture.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation spanning zero-shot camera pose estimation, dense point map estimation, large-scale visual localization, and monocular panoramic depth estimation, showing significant performance gains over perspective baselines (e.g., Stanford2D3D AUC@30 improves from ~2% to ~80%).

Drastic speedup in large-scale multi-view 360° localization and reconstruction (~3 seconds feed-forward) compared to traditional SfM/matching pipelines like IM360 and COLMAP variants (minutes to tens of minutes).
weaknesses: Methodological novelty is largely an integration of prior components: the spherical harmonics ray formulation follows UniK3D [54], the multi-view permutation-equivariant architecture and scale-alignment scheme follow $\pi^3$ [80], and calibration token conditioning has precedents in monocular depth literature [19].

Coarse camera conditioning: The model relies on discrete camera category tokens (pinhole, fisheye, 360°). Real-world fisheye and wide-angle lenses exhibit considerable variation in FoV (e.g., 140° to 220°) and non-linear projection profiles (stereographic, equidistant, equisolid). The paper lacks analysis on how sensitive the model is to intra-category lens distortion variations when using a single shared 'fisheye' token.
Evaluation on pose estimation uses relatively small sampled sets (e.g., only 20 sampled sequences on Stanford2D3D), which may limit the statistical robustness of the zero-shot pose benchmark.

strengths: Addresses an important and practical limitation of current multi-view feed-forward 3D reconstruction models (such as DUSt3R, VGGT, and π³), which assume pinhole/rectified perspective cameras and degrade significantly on fisheye and omnidirectional 360° imagery.
Proposes a well-integrated formulation combining a permutation-equivariant multi-view pipeline with a spherical harmonics ray-space representation and explicit camera model token conditioning.

Extensive experimental evaluation across diverse tasks and wide FoV benchmarks (Zip-NeRF, FIORD, Stanford2D3D, Matterport3D, ScanNet++), demonstrating dramatic performance gains in pose estimation, point cloud reconstruction, and localization speed compared to traditional SfM pipelines and perspective-biased feed-forward baselines.
Informative ablation studies illustrating the benefit of cross-camera-type joint training, the importance of explicit camera model tokens, and the impact of sequence length during training.
weaknesses: The core technical components are largely a synthesis of prior designs: the ray-based spherical harmonics formulation is adopted from UniK3D, and the multi-view permutation-equivariant framework is adapted from π³.

The camera model token conditioning requires clearer specification. If the token is simply a categorical/discrete prompt (e.g., pinhole, fisheye, 360°), it requires user specification at test time and may struggle with varying lens characteristics within the same category (e.g., varying fields of view from 150° to 220° or differing distortion models).

On the FIORD benchmark (Tables 2 and 3), the retrained π³ baseline (Ours (π³)) actually outperforms Wid3R on several pose metrics (e.g., AUC@30 of 72.56 vs. 68.20, and ATE of 0.32 vs. 0.44). The paper would benefit from a more thorough analysis of why the ray-based representation slightly underperforms the direct point regression head on this specific dataset.

strengths: Addresses an important and practical limitation in current feed-forward multi-view 3D reconstruction models (e.g., DUSt3R, VGGT, $\pi^3$), which fail or degrade significantly when applied to wide field-of-view (fisheye and $360^\circ$ equirectangular) imagery.

Formulates a sound architecture by decomposing point estimation into ray directions (parameterized by spherical harmonics) and radial distance, integrated into a permutation-equivariant multi-view framework.

Comprehensive experimental validation across multiple benchmarks and camera types (fisheye on FIORD, Zip-NeRF; spherical on Matterport3D, Stanford2D3D), demonstrating consistent gains over both off-the-shelf and identically retrained multi-view baselines.

Demonstrates remarkable runtime efficiency for large-scale indoor 3D localization and reconstruction (producing 3D representations in ~3 seconds compared to dozens of minutes for optimization-based SfM pipelines like IM360).
weaknesses: The technical novelty is somewhat modular: the architecture largely combines the permutation-equivariant backbone of $\pi^3$ with the spherical harmonics ray formulation of UniK3D and discrete camera conditioning tokens.

The paper claims reconstruction 'without explicit calibration', yet the network requires a discrete camera model token (pinhole, fisheye, 360). The paper lacks analysis regarding robustness to token mis-specification or handling varying distortion profiles within the same general category (e.g., different fisheye lens geometries).

Architectural and implementation details regarding the camera model token are brief (e.g., token dimensionality, injection mechanism into the transformer layers, and behavior when handling heterogeneous mixtures of camera types within a single sequence).

strengths: Addresses an important and practical limitation of current feed-forward 3D reconstruction models (e.g., DUSt3R, VGGT, $\pi^3$), which inherently assume pinhole/rectified camera geometry and fail on wide field-of-view and 360-degree imagery.

Provides extensive quantitative and qualitative validation across a diverse set of indoor and outdoor benchmarks (ScanNet++, Matterport3D, Stanford2D3D, FIORD, Zip-NeRF), demonstrating substantial improvements over baseline models in camera pose estimation, point cloud reconstruction, and monocular depth.

Demonstrates notable efficiency in large-scale visual localization and mapping on Matterport3D, achieving feed-forward reconstruction in seconds compared to conventional SfM pipelines that take tens of minutes.
Includes informative ablation experiments examining the benefits of multi-camera joint training, camera model token prompting, batch size scaling, and attention mechanisms.
weaknesses: The core technical originality is somewhat incremental, as the spherical harmonics-based ray parameterization and asymmetric ray loss are directly adopted from UniK3D, while the multi-view permutation-equivariant framework is adapted from $\pi^3$. The technical novelty essentially lies in the integration of these two ideas and the addition of camera model prompt tokens.

The camera conditioning mechanism requires manual specification of a discrete camera model token (e.g., pinhole, fisheye, 360) at test time. The paper lacks analysis on how the model behaves under token mismatch, intermediate/arbitrary fields of view, or uncalibrated scenarios where the exact camera category is unknown.

Architectural and implementation details regarding the camera token conditioning are underexplained in the main text; it is unclear whether the camera token is prepended to transformer patch sequences, applied via cross-attention, or injected through adaptive layer normalization.

The evaluation protocols rely heavily on ground-truth-dependent optimal scale alignment ($s^*$) for both point clouds and relative camera translations (Eq. 2, Eq. 7), leaving open questions about the model's capability to deliver consistent metric scale across diverse sensor types without ground-truth fitting.
